USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold existing tariffs in place as leverage but do not escalate further. Actively signal willingness to resume negotiations before List 4 takes effect September 1, using the month-long window as a diplomatic off-ramp. The currency manipulator designation should be used as leverage at the IMF and in bilateral talks, not as a pretext for additional tariff rounds.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is genuine but not existential (threat_score 0.35). On the damage side: the Dow plunged 760 points on August 5 in its worst day of 2019; $1.4 trillion in S&P value was wiped out in under a week (CNBC, Aug 6). The yield curve inverted to its widest since 2007, flashing a recession signal (Wharton, Aug 6). Tariffs are already costing US households over $1,200/year (CNN, Aug 2). China has suspended ALL US agricultural purchases as of August 5-6, a 'body blow' to farmers already reeling from the trade war — farm exports collapsed from $19.5B (2017) to $9.1B (2018) per the American Farm Bureau. List 4 would hit consumer electronics, apparel, and toys directly, with economists warning of 'permanently higher prices' and reduced US firm competitiveness (Wharton analysis). The Huawei Entity List, while strategically useful, has created significant disruption for US chip suppliers, with the Temporary General License expiring August 19 adding urgency.

On the leverage side: China's economy is slowing and the yuan breach of 7/USD signals their pain. The currency manipulator designation gives the US diplomatic tools. Bipartisan support exists — Schumer endorsed the designation. Tariffs now cover ~$550B of Chinese imports, giving maximum negotiating pressure.

However, further escalation risks are substantial. The trade war has become a currency war (Peterson Institute's Bergsten, Aug 6). China retains asymmetric retaliation tools: rare earth leverage (Xi's Jiangxi visit May 20), the unreliable entity list (announced May 31), and regulatory harassment of US firms operating in China. Penn Wharton modeling shows the tariff war is 'doing permanent damage to the US economy' by reducing foreign capital inflows and eroding US firm competitiveness globally. US companies are relocating supply chains not to the US but to higher-cost alternatives in Asia — a permanent efficiency loss.

The action_score of -0.15 reflects mild forward pressure: maintain the existing tariff architecture as leverage, resist domestic hawks pushing for immediate List 4 escalation to 25%, and use the September 1 deadline as a natural negotiation catalyst. This is not concession — it is strategic patience. The opponent is under more pressure than we are, but the costs of further escalation to both sides make a negotiated outcome preferable to mutual attrition.

After CNY breaks 7 per USD, US Treasury designates China a currency manipulator (first such designation since 1994)
Dow plunges 760 points in worst day of 2019 as trade war intensifies. $1.4 trillion S&P wipeout in under a week.
Penn Wharton Budget Model: escalating trade war leads to dire results. Permanent damage to US economy, reduced foreign capital inflows, lower wages.
China has halted its purchases of U.S. agricultural products and will not rule out levying import tariffs on American farm imports purchased after Aug. 3.
Tariffs already costing typical US household more than $1,200 a year. List 4 will hit consumer electronics, clothing, shoes, toys.
The bigger point is that this is another escalating step whereby these two countries seem to be diverging further rather than making some attempts at finding some way out.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain current retaliatory posture — the agricultural purchase suspension and currency flexibility are calibrated responses already in play. Do not escalate further with new measures (rare earth ban, broader export controls) as this risks triggering additional US sanctions. Signal willingness to resume talks in September as planned. Use the ~3-week window before List 4 takes effect to prepare domestic stimulus and let the currency adjustment partially offset tariff impact.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high and escalating. GDP growth hit a 27-year low of 6.2% in Q2 2019 (CNN, July 15). Exports to the US fell 8.1% YoY in H1 2019, imports from the US plunged 30% (CNN). The Huawei Entity List placement (May 16) directly attacks China's most prominent tech firm and threatens access to critical US semiconductor and software inputs (Wired, June 17). On August 1, Trump announced List 4 tariffs of 10% on the remaining ~$300B of Chinese goods effective September 1 (event timeline), which would bring virtually all Chinese exports to the US under tariff coverage. On August 5, the PBOC allowed the yuan to breach 7/USD — a significant psychological level — and the US Treasury formally designated China a currency manipulator for the first time since 1994 (Treasury press release SM751, Aug 5). While the currency manipulator label is largely symbolic for now (OPIC/procurement penalties don't kick in for a year per statute), it opens a pathway for the Commerce Department to treat currency undervaluation as an illegal trade subsidy, potentially triggering countervailing duties (Politico, Aug 6). China has already retaliated by suspending US agricultural purchases and has signaled rare earth leverage (Xi's May 20 visit to Jiangxi REE facility; Xinhua editorial May 29). However, a full rare earth ban would damage China's reputation as a reliable supplier and accelerate US diversification efforts (CRS report IF11259, June 2019). The IMF cut China's 2019 growth forecast to 6.2% and warned that 25% tariffs across the board would 'affect growth significantly' (Reuters, June 5). Beijing has room for fiscal/monetary stimulus — the PBOC has cut reserve requirements six times since early 2018 and the IMF judged current stimulus 'sufficient to stabilise growth' absent further escalation. The action_score of -0.15 reflects that China has already deployed meaningful retaliatory measures (ag purchases halt, currency flexibility) and should hold firm without introducing new escalation vectors, preserving the option for September talks while the List 4 deadline creates natural leverage.

US Treasury currency manipulator designation (Aug 5) — symbolic but opens pathway to countervailing duties
Yuan breached 7/USD (Aug 5) — PBOC effectively weaponized exchange rate
China already retaliating: agricultural purchase suspension, currency flexibility, rare earth signaling
IMF warns 25% across-board tariffs would significantly impact growth
Domestic stimulus toolkit available: RRR cuts, infrastructure spending, tax cuts

sources_cited.excerpt: After the Shanghai round, Trump announces 10% tariffs on the remaining ~$300B of Chinese goods (List 4), effective Sept 1.
After CNY breaks 7 per USD, US Treasury designates China a currency manipulator (first such designation since 1994).
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.

China's GDP grew at 6.2% in Q2 2019, the slowest quarterly growth rate since 1992. Exports to the United States decreased 8.1% for the first half of 2019. Imports from the United States plunged 30% year on year.
IMF cut China's 2019 GDP growth forecast to 6.2%. 'Let me make it clear, if tariffs do go up to say 25% across the board, growth would be affected significantly.'
Secretary Mnuchin has determined that China is a Currency Manipulator. 'China has taken concrete steps to devalue its currency, while maintaining substantial foreign exchange reserves.'
Xi Jinping toured a rare earth processing facility. A Xinhua editorial warned that by waging a trade war, the US risks losing supply of materials vital to sustaining its technological strength.

Commerce Department has previously proposed treating undervalued currencies as an illegal trade subsidy. If that becomes final, Treasury's designation could help open the floodgates to countervailing duties on Chinese goods.
